Extended AABA.reason: Catalog line 32. AABABA matches the catalogued extended return. Compound AABA describes internal formal organization, often entire verse–chorus units inside A sections.

Verse-refrain with introductory verse.reason: Catalog line 34. The history and staging of Tin Pan Alley or minstrel repertory do not define the optional introductory verse and main refrain combination.

12-bar blues.reason: Catalog line 35. AAB describes the words of a blues stanza. Twelve bars measure a musical cycle; the source's 16-bar example also uses a stretched blues stanza.

Simple verse-chorus.reason: Catalog line 38. ABAB states alternation without the shared harmonic plan distinguishing simple from contrasting verse–chorus.

Verse-prechorus-chorus.reason: Catalog line 40. Channel and climb label the preparatory section rather than the three-section cycle.

Verse-chorus-bridge.reason: Catalog line 41. ABABCB maps A to verse, B to chorus and C to bridge; the second formula ABCABCDC has four symbols with no mapping to the stated three sections.

Verse-chorus with post-chorus.reason: Catalog line 42. Modern pop form does not identify a post-chorus; other catalog entries also describe contemporary pop layouts.

Chorus-first.reason: Catalog line 43. A hook can occur outside a chorus. Opening on a hook alone does not establish that the chorus comes first.

Verse-chorus with solo.reason: Catalog line 44. ‘Rock or country form with a break’ gives a stylistic context and optional break; a break need not be the solo described by this form.

Multi-part suite.reason: Catalog line 51. Mini-opera and epic describe other entities. The catalog explicitly defines Epic elsewhere by a heroic narrative, while a suite consists of linked sub-songs.

Contrafactum.reason: Catalog line 54. Fitting new words to an existing tune is the defining procedure, not a second name. Parody lyric adds a purpose not required by the definition.

Music-hall song.reason: Catalog line 57. Comic song and chorus song describe categories beyond the music-hall repertoire. The source itself allows narrative as well as comic verses.

Song-and-dance number.reason: Catalog line 59. Production number need not encode this particular dance break and return. The original entry specifies both.

Musical scene.reason: Catalog line 60. Extended number describes length and does not by itself identify the combination of dialogue, speech and song.

Duet dialogue song.reason: Catalog line 61. An answer song can be a separate recording answering an earlier song. Trading verses describes the two voices inside the entry's single performance.

Melodrama.reason: Catalog line 65. Spoken over music describes the technique rather than an alternate title for the form.

Head arrangement.reason: Catalog line 71. Head–solos–head describes a performance sequence. A head arrangement is devised and remembered by the musicians and can use different sequences.

Hip-hop verse-hook.reason: Catalog line 74. 16-and-8 names one bar-count pattern; the source explicitly permits other verse lengths. Rap song form also includes hookless tracks in this catalog.

Battle rap.reason: Catalog line 77. Written battle narrows the creation method. The source describes a contest, not a requirement that it be written.

Vamp / riff form.reason: Catalog line 81. Funk jam denotes a genre-specific example of a groove built on a repeating riff.

Gospel verse-chorus-vamp.reason: Catalog line 82. Drive section and quartet drive describe the gospel vamp portion of the sequence, not the entire verse–chorus–vamp form.

Traditional ballad.reason: Catalog line 93. Child ballad refers specifically to the body collected and classified by Francis James Child; traditional ballads exist beyond that collection.

Long-measure ballad.reason: Catalog line 94 conflates four tetrameter lines with paired fourteeners. Dividing paired fourteeners gives a different measure.

Incremental-repetition ballad.reason: Catalog line 96. A question-and-answer exchange is frequent rather than required. Lord Randal and Edward are individual ballads.

Luck-visit / begging song.reason: Catalog line 107. Wassailing, souling, pace-egging, wren songs and May carols are distinct customs or associated songs. The catalog groups them by the door-to-door visit.

Dirge / lament.reason: Catalog line 109. Keen and coronach identify particular lament traditions. The heading covers mourning songs more broadly.

Zipper song.reason: Catalog line 121. Slot is the place where a word changes in the verse template. It is a component of the operation.

Cumulative song.reason: Catalog line 122. Twelve Days, Old Lady and House That Jack Built are examples, not additional names for the form.

Counting song.reason: Catalog line 123. Green Grow the Rushes O and Dilly Song identify particular songs in the counting repertoire.

Countdown song.reason: Catalog line 124. Ten Green Bottles is the named song example, not an alternate name for countdown songs.

Nonsense-refrain song.reason: Catalog line 126. A diddling chorus is a possible refrain; the enclosing song includes other material.

Counting-out rhyme.reason: Catalog line 129. Eeny-meeny identifies a particular traditional rhyme or incipit; others use different words.

Skipping / clapping rhyme.reason: Jump-rope rhyme identifies the skipping subtype. Clapping rhymes can accompany a different game.

Singing game.reason: Catalog line 131. Ring games and play-party songs are specific kinds of games or repertoire rather than names for every singing game.

Finger play.reason: Catalog line 132. Action rhyme covers movements by many parts of the body; a finger play is a narrower gestural case.

Madrigal.reason: Catalog line 143. English madrigal qualifies a national repertoire within the broader heading. The catalog's remit already specifies English-language material.

Part-song (Victorian).reason: Catalog line 150. Partsong is a spelling of the general term. The catalog's Madrigal and Ballett rows also call those works part-songs. The unqualified spelling cannot identify the Victorian subtype uniquely.

Metrical hymn.reason: Catalog line 156. ‘Hymn in CM, LM, SM and other metres’ lists alternative metres within the form.

Camp-meeting song.reason: Catalog line 159. Wandering refrain names material that can travel among songs. It is not an alternate name for a complete camp-meeting song.

Praise chorus.reason: Catalog line 160. Scripture chorus narrows the text source. The entry can also be defined by a short repeating praise text and tag.

Metrical psalm.reason: Catalog line 166. Psalm paraphrase does not specify verse, meter or a tune; the catalogued type imposes metrical stanzas.

Anglican chant.reason: Catalog line 168. A pointed psalm is text marked for chanting. The chant itself supplies the repeated musical formula.

Psalm with antiphon.reason: Catalog line 169. Psalm tone is the melodic formula for chanting verses. The antiphon is a different constituent of the whole.

Litany.reason: Catalog line 172. Intercession is a purpose shared by many prayers. A litany here uses a sequence of petitions and responses.

Canticle.reason: Catalog line 174. Magnificat, Nunc Dimittis and Te Deum are distinct service texts within the canticle repertoire.

Doxology.reason: Catalog line 175. Gloria Patri and Ken's doxology are individual texts; the praise formula is the category.

Shape-note anthem.reason: Catalog line 179. Sacred Harp anthem refers to repertoire associated with one named hymnal and tradition. The heading identifies the notation, a broader criterion.

Anglican service.reason: Catalog line 181. Great Service and Short Service designate different settings or subtypes within the heading.

American sonnet.reason: Catalog line 199. The source explicitly permits loose rhyme as well as no rhyme. Unrhymed sonnet fails as an equivalent for that range.

Tanka.reason: Catalog line 240. Waka can denote tanka in later usage, but historically is broader. The Academy identifies tanka as a form of waka.

Renga / renku.reason: This traditional name corresponds to the renku side of the heading. Haikai has broader senses, and kasen is a particular layout. Both remain available as search terms.

Englyn.reason: Catalog line 257. Penfyr, milwr and unodl union are distinct englyn forms with different templates.

Byr a thoddaid.reason: Catalog line 262. Toddaid is a constituent two-line unit; the whole form also includes cyhydedd fer material.

Irish syllabic quatrains.reason: Catalog line 266. Deibhidhe, rannaigheacht, séadna and ae freislighe are individual meters with different rhythms or rhyme conditions.

Couplet.reason: Catalog line 297. Rhymed couplet qualifies a common subtype. While definitions vary, the Academy explicitly permits unrhymed couplets; this catalog's elegiac couplet row also says usually unrhymed.

Heroic couplet.reason: Catalog line 298. Closed describes the syntax ending with the pair; heroic specifies iambic pentameter. Heroic couplets can enjamb.

Octosyllabic couplet.reason: Catalog line 299. Eight syllables measures length; tetrameter counts four feet. The counts coincide in some meters only.

Fourteener.reason: Catalog line 302. Fourteen syllables is the source's length requirement; heptameter counts feet and does not on its own specify fourteen syllables.

Tercet.reason: Catalog line 308. Triad broadly means a set of three. The Pindaric ode entry, for example, uses triad for strophe, antistrophe and epode rather than a three-line stanza.

Sicilian tercet.reason: Catalog line 310. Enclosed tercet states ABA rhyme. It does not establish the pentameter required by the catalog row.

Common metre (CM).reason: Catalog line 314. Hymn metre describes a family that also includes Long metre and Short metre. Retain the common-metre count as a lookup notation.

Trochaic hymn metres.reason: Catalog line 321. The listed numerical patterns are alternative named realizations of the family, not aliases of the aggregate.

Other named hymn metres.reason: Catalog line 322. The seven distinct syllabic recipes catalogue members of an otherwise unspecified group, not seven names for one meter.

In Memoriam stanza.reason: Catalog line 324. Envelope quatrain identifies its enclosing ABBA rhyme; the In Memoriam stanza also specifies tetrameter.

Sapphic stanza.reason: Catalog line 328. Sapphic hymn stanza is a hymnic use. Preserve the displayed count as shorthand for this source's line-length pattern, without assigning every such hymn the classical meter.

Décima espinela.reason: Catalog line 345. Décima covers more ten-line stanzas than the specific espinela with its ABBAACCDDC scheme.

Alliterative verse.reason: Catalog line 353. Old English line is one historical realization of emphasis through alliteration. It does not name all alliterative verse.

Accentual verse.reason: Catalog line 354. Dolnik imposes restrictions on the intervals between strong stresses. The broader catalog form permits variable intervening syllables.

Elegy.reason: Mourning is a shared subject. The traditional first stage and a narrower pastoral kind do not name the whole category.

Eclogue.reason: Catalog line 378. An exchange of shepherds' speeches is the catalog's pastoral setup. Amoebean dialogue identifies alternating responses; it does not identify the whole pastoral genre.

Aisling.reason: Catalog line 382. Vision poem is broader than the source's specific Irish encounter and prophecy.

Gnomic verse.reason: Catalog line 385. Maxims are the short statements collected in a gnomic poem. A maxim is not necessarily verse.

Pattern poem.reason: Catalog line 393. An altar poem arranges its text in a particular shape. Other shapes, including the wings in the source's own example, remain pattern poems.

Acrostic.reason: Catalog line 398. Double acrostic and telestich distinguish positional mechanisms, rather than renaming an ordinary initial-letter acrostic.

Exquisite corpse.reason: Catalog line 410. Collaborative verse names a broad process shared with rengay and other entries. Exquisite corpse also limits how much prior text each contributor sees.

Triadic line.reason: Stepping is visible layout. A variable foot is a proposed unit of measure and needs independent evidence.

Ternary.reason: Catalog line 46. Da capo song is an applicable return pattern in some ternary songs; da capo itself is a repeat instruction and does not cover every ternary form. Index the narrower connection as a search association.

Quodlibet.reason: Catalog line 53. Partner song describes the pedagogical setting in which independent melodies combine. The overlap with quodlibet does not establish the two terms as equivalent across all repertoires. Index the association separately.

Barbershop tag.reason: Catalog line 73. The bare name tag has a barbershop sense and a broader ending sense. Offer search in context while keeping generic section tags distinct from the standalone barbershop excerpt.

Call-and-response.reason: A leader and answering group define this catalog entry. Alternation between two choirs can also be antiphonal and has a different distribution of voices.

Nursery rhyme.reason: A regional nursery-rhyme name contains a named figure. Keep the display and general search independent of named examples.

Lined-out hymn.reason: Lining out names a technique that can be used to sing a hymn. Search can find the hymn through that technique. The catalog also gives an eponym for a narrower repertoire.

Ring shout.reason: Shout can name this practice in its tradition. Bare shout also describes a vocal action, so the search term carries the ring-shout performance context.

Rondeau prime.reason: The same twelve positions occur under both names. Refrain treatment and period-specific terminology limit interchangeability.

Rondine.reason: The same twelve positions occur under both names. Refrain treatment and period-specific terminology limit interchangeability.

Stornello.reason: This regional term for the whole song also has independent musical uses for a recurring section. The regional qualifier identifies the intended meaning.

Ruthless rhyme.reason: The inventory’s recurring character is an example. A macabre subject alone is insufficient to establish another name as a synonym for the entire body of verse.

Sicilian octave.reason: The regional name identifies the alternating eight-line pattern. The umbrella term strambotto also covers regional forms with other rhyme schemes.

Heroic quatrain.reason: The second source alias is an unverified eponym; the surviving alternate name identifies the four-line stanza in this context.
